Yes. I would make this a **different analysis from the previous one**. The central quantities become:

* `SampleMolPct`: each lipid species as % of all measured lipid molecules in that sample.
* `ClassMolPct`: each lipid class as % of all measured lipid molecules in that sample.
* `WithinClassPct`: each lipid species as % of its own lipid class.

The third quantity is the key one for compensation. If total PC stays similar but PC shifts from 34:1/36:1 toward 36:4/38:4, that is a strong **within-class remodelling phenotype** even though total PC barely changes.

Below is an R Markdown-ready workflow.

---

# 1. Setup

```{R}
# ============================================================
# LTP KO LIBRARY
# COMPOSITIONAL LIPID + SATURATION REMODELLING ANALYSIS
# ============================================================

library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)
library(ggthemes)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = F,warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,fig.width = 10,fig.height = 7
)

theme_set(
  theme_base(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey95")
    )
)

options(dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# SETTINGS
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Change this to the name(s) of your control samples.
#
# IMPORTANT:
# Controls are NOT used for normalization.
# They are only used later as a biological reference
# when asking whether a KO composition differs from normal.

CONTROL_GENES <- paste0("NonTarget_", 1:6)   # <-- EDIT


# For detecting compensation:
#
# "controls"       = compare the within-sample-normalized
#                    composition to controls
#
# "library_median" = compare each LTP to the median
#                    composition of the complete screen

REFERENCE_MODE <- "controls"


# Manual exclusions.
#
# Run the QC section first.
# Then add problematic samples/genes here and rerun.

EXCLUDE_GENES <- c(
  # "GENE1",
  # "GENE2"
)

EXCLUDE_SAMPLE_KEYS <- c(
  # "GENE1__Sample1__Extraction1__Roster1"
)


# Number of biological replicates we ideally want
MIN_REPLICATES <- 2

# Replicate correlation below this is worth inspecting.
MIN_REPLICATE_CORRELATION <- 0.70


# Compensation thresholds.
# A class is considered "stable" when its abundance differs
# by less than:
# max(1 percentage point, 20% of its reference abundance)

CLASS_STABILITY_MIN_PP <- 1
CLASS_STABILITY_RELATIVE <- 0.20


# At least this much of the within-class saturation
# distribution must be rearranged.

MIN_REDISTRIBUTION_PERCENT <- 10

# Replicate saturation profiles should point in approximately
# the same direction.

MIN_PROFILE_AGREEMENT <- 0.50


# Heatmap sizes
TOP_N_SPECIES <- 50
```

# 2. Prepare the raw data

```{R}
# ============================================================
# DATA PREPARATION
# ============================================================
acyls1 = read_csv("~/Desktop/GitProjects/ltp_library_analysis/data/LTP_acyl_concentrations_raw1.csv")

acyls1 <- acyls1 %>% 
   mutate(X = paste0(Class, "(",Tails,")")) 


acyls_raw <- acyls1[-1] %>%
   mutate(
      Gene = as.character(Target.Gene.Symbol), 
      LipidSpecies = as.character(X),
      Class = as.character(Class),
      nmol = as.numeric(nmolg), 
      TotalDB = as.numeric(Total_tail_bend), 
      TotalLength = as.numeric(Total_tail_length),
      Tail1DB = as.numeric(Tail_1_bend),
      Tail2DB = as.numeric(Tail_2_bend),
      Tail1Length = as.numeric(Tail_1_length),
      Tail2Length = as.numeric(Tail_2_length),
      ExpectedTails = readr::parse_number(as.character(Tails)),
      Group = if_else(Gene %in% CONTROL_GENES, "CTRL", "KO"),
      SampleKey = paste(Gene, SampleID, Extraction, Roster, sep = "__"),
      Feature = paste(Class, LipidSpecies, sep = " | ")
   ) %>%
   filter(!is.na(Gene),
          !is.na(Class),
          !is.na(LipidSpecies),
          is.finite(nmol),
          nmol >= 0)
```

Check the samples:

```{R}
acyls_raw %>% 
  distinct(
    Gene, SampleID, Extraction, Roster, SampleKey
  ) %>%
  arrange(Gene,SampleID) %>%
  print(n = Inf)
```

# 3. Function for within-sample normalization

This is now the core of the analysis.

```{R}
make_species_table <- function(dat) {

  dat %>%

    group_by(
      SampleKey,
      Gene,
      Group,
      LBP_Family,
      SampleID,
      Extraction,
      Roster,
      Type2,
      Class,
      LipidSpecies,
      Feature,
      Tails,
      Tail_1,
      Tail1Length,
      Tail1DB,
      Tail_2,
      Tail2Length,
      Tail2DB,
      TotalLength,
      TotalDB,
      ExpectedTails
    ) %>%

    summarise(
      nmol =
        sum(
          nmol,
          na.rm = TRUE
        ),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%

    # ---------------------------------
    # FIRST NORMALIZATION:
    # each species as fraction of
    # the complete sample lipidome
    # ---------------------------------

    group_by(
      SampleKey
    ) %>%

    mutate(
      SampleTotalNmol =sum(nmol,na.rm = TRUE),
      SampleMolFraction = nmol / SampleTotalNmol,
      SampleMolPct =
        100 *
        SampleMolFraction
    ) %>%

    ungroup() %>%

    # ---------------------------------
    # SECOND NORMALIZATION:
    # species as fraction of its class
    #
    # This is used for saturation
    # redistribution / compensation.
    # ---------------------------------

    group_by(
      SampleKey,
      Class
    ) %>%

    mutate(

      ClassNmol =
        sum(
          nmol,
          na.rm = TRUE
        ),

      ClassMolPct =
        100 *
        ClassNmol /
        first(
          SampleTotalNmol
        ),

      WithinClassFraction =
        nmol /
        ClassNmol,

      WithinClassPct =
        100 *
        WithinClassFraction
    ) %>%

    ungroup()
}
```

Initial normalization, before exclusions:

```{R}
species_initial <-
  make_species_table(
    acyls_raw
  )



```

Check that each sample sums to 100%:

```{R}
species_initial %>%
  group_by(
    SampleKey
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    TotalPct =
      sum(
        SampleMolPct
      ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  summary()
```

These should all be approximately `100`.

---

# 4. QC before excluding anything

Because the analysis is compositional, I would assess replicate similarity using a **CLR-like transformation of the within-sample proportions**, rather than raw nmol.

```{R}
# ============================================================
# QC
# ============================================================

clr_transform <- function(x) {
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  positive <-
    x[
      is.finite(x) &
      x > 0
    ]
  if (length(positive) == 0) {
    return(
      rep(
        0,
        length(x)
      )
    )
  }

  pseudo <-
    min(positive) / 2
  lx <-
    log(
      x +
      pseudo
    )

  lx -
    mean(lx)
}


safe_cor <- function(x, y) {
  ok <-
    is.finite(x) & is.finite(y)

  if (sum(ok) < 5)
    return(NA_real_)

  if (
    sd(x[ok]) == 0 || sd(y[ok]) == 0
  )
    return(NA_real_)

  cor(
    x[ok],
    y[ok],
    method = "spearman"
  )
}
```

Create sample × species matrix:

```{R}
qc_wide <- species_initial %>%
  group_by(
    SampleKey,
    Feature
  ) %>%

  summarise(
    SampleMolPct =
      sum(
        SampleMolPct
      ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%

  pivot_wider(
    names_from =
      Feature,
    values_from =
      SampleMolPct,
    values_fill = 0
  )


qc_ids <-
  qc_wide$SampleKey


qc_matrix <-
  qc_wide %>%
  select(
    -SampleKey
  ) %>%
  as.matrix()


rownames(qc_matrix) <- qc_ids


qc_clr <-
  t(
    apply(
      qc_matrix,
      1,
      clr_transform
    )
  )
```

Sample metadata:

```{R}
sample_metadata <- species_initial %>%
  distinct(
    SampleKey,
    Gene,
    Group,
    SampleID,
    Extraction,
    Roster,
    LBP_Family
  )
```

# 5. Replicate-to-consensus correlation

For every replicate, compare its lipidome with the median of the other replicates for that same LTP.

```{R}
replicate_correlations <-
  map_dfr(
    unique(
      sample_metadata$Gene
    ),

    function(gene_i) {

      ids <-
        sample_metadata %>%
        filter(
          Gene == gene_i
        ) %>%
        pull(
          SampleKey
        )


      if (length(ids) < 2) {

        return(
          tibble(
            SampleKey = ids,
            ReplicateConsensusR =
              NA_real_
          )
        )
      }


      map_dfr(

        ids,

        function(id_i) {

          other_ids <-
            setdiff(
              ids,
              id_i
            )


          consensus <-
            apply(
              qc_clr[
                other_ids,
                ,
                drop = FALSE
              ],
              2,
              median,
              na.rm = TRUE
            )


          tibble(

            SampleKey =
              id_i,

            ReplicateConsensusR =
              safe_cor(
                qc_clr[
                  id_i,
                ],
                consensus
              )
          )
        }
      )
    }
  )
```

Sample totals:

```{R Sample totals}
qc_summary <- species_initial %>%

  group_by(
    SampleKey,
    Gene,
    Group,
    SampleID
  ) %>%

  summarise(

    TotalNmol =
      first(
        SampleTotalNmol
      ),

    DetectedSpecies =
      sum(
        nmol > 0
      ),

    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%

  left_join(
    replicate_correlations,
    by = "SampleKey"
  ) %>%

  mutate(

    BadReplicate =
      !is.na(
        ReplicateConsensusR
      ) &
      ReplicateConsensusR <
        MIN_REPLICATE_CORRELATION
  )
```

Plot:

```{R}
ggplot(
  qc_summary,
  aes(x = Gene, y = ReplicateConsensusR)) +
   geom_hline(yintercept = MIN_REPLICATE_CORRELATION, linetype = 2 ) +
  geom_point(aes(shape =BadReplicate),
    position =position_jitter(width = 0.15), size = 2.5) +
  geom_text_repel(data =
                     qc_summary %>%
                     filter(BadReplicate),
                  aes(label =paste0(Gene," / ",SampleID)),
                  size = 3,max.overlaps = Inf) +
   coord_flip() +
   labs(title ="Reproducibility of within-sample-normalized lipidomes",
        x = NULL,y ="Correlation with other replicates")
```

This is where I would identify the obviously non-reproducible samples.

Print their exact keys:

```{R}
qc_summary %>%
   filter(BadReplicate) %>%
   select(Gene,SampleID,SampleKey,ReplicateConsensusR) %>%
   arrange(ReplicateConsensusR) %>%
   print(n = Inf)
```

Then put the problematic ones into `EXCLUDE_SAMPLE_KEYS` at the top.

# 6. Apply exclusions and renormalize

This renormalization step is important: if a complete sample is removed, no issue. The percentages of the remaining samples are calculated independently anyway.

```{R}

   "GLTPD2__H45__H__45",
   "SEC14L2__J49__J__49"
)

acyls_clean <- acyls_raw %>%
  filter(
    !Gene %in% EXCLUDE_GENES,
    !SampleKey %in% EXCLUDE_SAMPLE_KEYS
  )

species <-
  make_species_table(
    acyls_clean
  )
```

# Part A — Overview of lipid classes

# 7. Class composition for each sample

```{R}
class_sample <- species %>%
  group_by(
    SampleKey,
    Gene,
    Group,
    LBP_Family,
    SampleID,
    Extraction,
    Roster,
    Class
  ) %>%

  summarise(

    ClassNmol =
      sum(
        nmol,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    ClassMolPct =
      sum(
        SampleMolPct,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Thus:

[
\text{ClassMolPct}
==================

100\times
\frac{\sum \text{nmol within class}}
{\sum \text{nmol all lipids}}
]

No control normalization is involved.

# 10. Relative class abnormalities across the library

The absolute plot is dominated by naturally abundant classes such as PC.

For detecting unusual LTP phenotypes, make another heatmap that scales **each class across the library**.

This is visualization only. It is not control normalization.

```{R Relative class abnormalities across the library}
class_gene_z <- class_gene %>%
  group_by(
    Class
  ) %>%

  mutate(

    ClassMedian =
      median(
        MedianClassPct,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    ClassMAD =
      mad(
        MedianClassPct,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    ClassZ =
      if_else(
        ClassMAD > 0,
        (
          MedianClassPct -
          ClassMedian
        ) /
          ClassMAD,
        0
      )
  ) %>%

  ungroup()
```

```{R}
ggplot(
  class_gene_z,
  aes(x = Class,y = Gene,fill = ClassZ)
) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(midpoint = 0,name ="Robust\nz-score") +
  labs(
    title =
      "Relative lipid-class phenotypes",
    subtitle =
      "Values are scaled within each lipid class across the complete library",
    x = NULL,y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y =element_text(size = 6))

library(ggbeeswarm)
#plot by BC
ggplot(
  class_gene_z,
  aes(x = Class ,y = ClassZ)) +
  geom_quasirandom(shape = 21, aes(fill = ClassZ)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(midpoint = 0,name ="Robust\nz-score") +
  labs(
    title =
      "Relative lipid-class phenotypes",
    subtitle =
      "Values are scaled within each lipid class across the complete library",
    x = NULL,y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y =element_text(size = 6)) +
   geom_text_repel(data = 
                      class_gene_z %>% 
                      filter(abs(ClassZ) > 3), 
                   aes(label = Gene, color = Class))


```

This should make things such as the ORP9/ORP11 SM phenotype much easier to see than the absolute mol-% plot.

```{R}
  group_by(Feature) %>%
  summarise(
    Variability =

    .groups = "drop"

  slice_max(Variability,n =TOP_N_SPECIES) %>%
  pull(Feature)
```

# Part C — Saturation rearrangement

There are two useful ways of doing this.

### Analysis 1: whole lipid species

Use:

```text
Total_tail_bend
```

For example:

* PC(16:0/18:0) → DB0
* PC(16:0/18:1) → DB1
* PC(18:1/18:1) → DB2
* PC(16:0/20:4) → DB4

This works even when individual acyl chains cannot be fully resolved.

### Analysis 2: individual resolved chains

Use:

```text
Tail_1_bend
Tail_2_bend
```

This distinguishes genuinely polyunsaturated chains from two MUFA chains.

I would perform both.

---

# 13. Molecular saturation category

```{R}
DB_LEVELS <- c(
  "DB0",
  "DB1",
  "DB2",
  "DB3",
  "DB4",
  "DB5",
  "DB6+"
)


species_sat <- species %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(
      TotalDB
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    DBbin = case_when(
      TotalDB == 0 ~ "DB0",
      TotalDB == 1 ~ "DB1",
      TotalDB == 2 ~ "DB2",
      TotalDB == 3 ~ "DB3",
      TotalDB == 4 ~ "DB4",
      TotalDB == 5 ~ "DB5",
      TotalDB >= 6 ~ "DB6+"
    ),
    DBbin =
      factor(DBbin,levels =DB_LEVELS),
    DBperTail =
      if_else(!is.na(ExpectedTails) & ExpectedTails > 0,
        TotalDB / ExpectedTails, NA_real_)
    )
```

---

# 14. Saturation distribution within each lipid class

This uses `WithinClassPct`.

Therefore PC always sums to 100%, PE always sums to 100%, etc.

```{R}
sat_raw <- species_sat %>%

  group_by(
    SampleKey,
    Gene,
    Group,
    LBP_Family,
    SampleID,
    Extraction,
    Roster,
    Class,
    DBbin
  ) %>%

  summarise(

    BinPct =
      sum(
        WithinClassPct,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Create all missing DB categories explicitly as zero:

```{R}
sample_class_grid <- species_sat %>%

  distinct(
    SampleKey,
    Gene,
    Group,
    LBP_Family,
    SampleID,
    Extraction,
    Roster,
    Class
  ) %>%

  crossing(
    DBbin =
      factor(
        DB_LEVELS,
        levels =
          DB_LEVELS
      )
  )


sat_sample <- sample_class_grid %>%
  left_join(
    sat_raw,
    by = c(
      "SampleKey",
      "Gene",
      "Group",
      "LBP_Family",
      "SampleID",
      "Extraction",
      "Roster",
      "Class",
      "DBbin"
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    BinPct = replace_na(BinPct,0))
```

---

# 15. Median saturation distribution per LTP

```{R}
sat_gene <- sat_sample %>%

  group_by(
    Gene,
    LBP_Family,
    Class,
    DBbin
  ) %>%

  summarise(

    MedianBinPct =
      median(
        BinPct,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    IQRBinPct =
      IQR(
        BinPct,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    n =
      n_distinct(
        SampleKey
      ),

    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%

  # Median of each bin separately may not add to
  # exactly 100, so renormalize the median profile.
  group_by(
    Gene,
    Class
  ) %>%

  mutate(
    MedianBinPct =
      100 *
      MedianBinPct /
      sum(
        MedianBinPct
      )
  ) %>%

  ungroup()
```

# 18. Continuous saturation metrics

Rather than only bins, calculate average unsaturation.

```{R}
saturation_metrics <- species_sat %>%

  group_by(
    SampleKey,
    Gene,
    Group,
    LBP_Family,
    SampleID,
    Extraction,
    Roster,
    Class
  ) %>%

  summarise(

    MeanTotalDB =
      weighted.mean(
        TotalDB,
        w = nmol,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    MeanDBperTail =
      weighted.mean(
        DBperTail,
        w = nmol,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    MeanTotalLength =
      weighted.mean(
        TotalLength,
        w = nmol,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    FullySaturatedSpeciesPct =
      100 *
      sum(
        nmol[
          TotalDB == 0
        ],
        na.rm = TRUE
      ) /
      sum(
        nmol,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    DB4plusSpeciesPct =
      100 *
      sum(
        nmol[
          TotalDB >= 4
        ],
        na.rm = TRUE
      ) /
      sum(
        nmol,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Median by LTP:

```{R}
saturation_metrics_gene <-
  saturation_metrics %>%

  group_by(
    Gene,
    LBP_Family,
    Class
  ) %>%

  summarise(

    MeanDBperTail =
      median(
        MeanDBperTail,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    MeanTotalDB =
      median(
        MeanTotalDB,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    SaturatedPct =
      median(
        FullySaturatedSpeciesPct,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    DB4plusPct =
      median(
        DB4plusSpeciesPct,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Heatmap:

```{R}
ggplot(
  saturation_metrics_gene,
  aes(
    x = Class,
    y = Gene,
    fill = MeanDBperTail
  )
) +

  geom_tile() +

  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name =
      "Mean DB\nper tail"
  ) +

  labs(
    title =

    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +

  theme(
    axis.text.y =
      element_text(

      )
  )
```

---

# Part D — Explicitly detect saturation compensation

This is the part I think is scientifically most interesting.

The logic is:

> **Class abundance stable + internal saturation profile substantially rearranged + replicates agree = candidate compensatory remodelling.**

No lipid value is normalized against the control. The control is simply the reference composition.

---

# 19. Define the reference composition

```{R}
has_controls <-
  any(
    species$Gene %in%
      CONTROL_GENES
  )


REFERENCE_MODE_USED <-
  REFERENCE_MODE


if (
  REFERENCE_MODE ==
  "controls" &&
  !has_controls
) {

  warning(
    "No CONTROL_GENES detected. Using library median instead."
  )

  REFERENCE_MODE_USED <-
    "library_median"
}
```

Class abundance reference:

```{R}
if (
  REFERENCE_MODE_USED ==
  "controls"
) {

  reference_class <- class_sample %>%

    filter(
      Gene %in%
        CONTROL_GENES
    ) %>%

    group_by(
      Class
    ) %>%

    summarise(
      RefClassPct =
        median(
          ClassMolPct,
          na.rm = TRUE
        ),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

} else {

  reference_class <- class_sample %>%

    group_by(
      Class
    ) %>%

    summarise(
      RefClassPct =
        median(
          ClassMolPct,
          na.rm = TRUE
        ),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}
```

Saturation reference:

```{R}
if (
  REFERENCE_MODE_USED ==
  "controls"
) {

  reference_sat <- sat_sample %>%

    filter(
      Gene %in%
        CONTROL_GENES
    ) %>%

    group_by(
      Class,
      DBbin
    ) %>%

    summarise(
      RefBinPct =
        median(
          BinPct,
          na.rm = TRUE
        ),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

} else {

  reference_sat <- sat_sample %>%

    group_by(
      Class,
      DBbin
    ) %>%

    summarise(
      RefBinPct =
        median(
          BinPct,
          na.rm = TRUE
        ),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}
```

Normalize the reference saturation profiles to 100%.

```{R}
reference_sat <- reference_sat %>%

  group_by(
    Class
  ) %>%

  mutate(
    RefBinPct =
      100 *
      RefBinPct /
      sum(
        RefBinPct
      )
  ) %>%

  ungroup()
```

---

# 20. Class-abundance change

Again, this is a **difference after sample normalization**, not a normalization to controls.

```{R}
class_difference <- class_sample %>%

  left_join(
    reference_class,
    by = "Class"
  ) %>%

  mutate(

    ClassDeltaPP =
      ClassMolPct -
      RefClassPct,

    AbsClassDeltaPP =
      abs(
        ClassDeltaPP
      )
  )
```

---

# 21. Saturation-profile change

```{R}
sat_difference <- sat_sample %>%

  left_join(
    reference_sat,
    by =
      c(
        "Class",
        "DBbin"
      )
  ) %>%

  mutate(
    BinDeltaPP =
      BinPct -
      RefBinPct
  )
```

---

# 22. Quantify redistribution

A very useful metric here is the **total variation distance**:

[
R =
\frac{1}{2}
\sum_i
|p_{KO,i} - p_{reference,i}|
]

Because the profiles sum to 100%, this has an intuitive interpretation.

If:

```text
RedistributionPct = 20
```

approximately 20% of that lipid class would have to be redistributed among saturation bins to convert the reference profile into the KO profile.

```{R}
redistribution_sample <- sat_difference %>%

  group_by(
    SampleKey,
    Gene,
    Group,
    LBP_Family,
    SampleID,
    Class
  ) %>%

  summarise(

    RedistributionPct =
      0.5 *
      sum(
        abs(
          BinDeltaPP
        ),
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Join class abundance:

```{R}
redistribution_sample <-
  redistribution_sample %>%

  left_join(

    class_difference %>%

      select(
        SampleKey,
        Class,
        ClassMolPct,
        RefClassPct,
        ClassDeltaPP,
        AbsClassDeltaPP
      ),

    by =
      c(
        "SampleKey",
        "Class"
      )
  )
```

---

# 23. Replicate agreement in the *direction* of saturation remodelling

Two samples can both have a high redistribution score while moving in completely opposite directions.

Therefore, I would explicitly compare their vectors:

```text
DB0 change
DB1 change
DB2 change
DB3 change
...
```

using cosine similarity.

```{R}
cosine_similarity <- function(x, y) {

  denom <-
    sqrt(
      sum(
        x^2
      )
    ) *
    sqrt(
      sum(
        y^2
      )
    )

  if (
    !is.finite(denom) ||
    denom == 0
  ) {
    return(
      NA_real_
    )
  }

  sum(
    x * y
  ) /
    denom
}
```

```{R}
median_pairwise_cosine <- function(d) {

  w <- d %>%

    select(
      SampleKey,
      DBbin,
      BinDeltaPP
    ) %>%

    pivot_wider(
      names_from =
        DBbin,
      values_from =
        BinDeltaPP,
      values_fill = 0
    )


  if (
    nrow(w) < 2
  )
    return(
      NA_real_
    )


  m <-
    w %>%
    select(
      -SampleKey
    ) %>%
    as.matrix()


  pairs <-
    combn(
      seq_len(
        nrow(m)
      ),
      2
    )


  similarities <-
    apply(
      pairs,
      2,
      function(idx) {

        cosine_similarity(
          m[
            idx[1],
          ],
          m[
            idx[2],
          ]
        )
      }
    )


  median(
    similarities,
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
}
```

Calculate it:

```{R}
profile_agreement <- sat_difference %>%

  filter(
    !Gene %in%
      CONTROL_GENES
  ) %>%

  group_by(
    Gene,
    Class
  ) %>%

  group_modify(
    ~ tibble(
      ProfileAgreement =
        median_pairwise_cosine(
          .x
        )
    )
  ) %>%

  ungroup()
```

Interpretation:

* near `+1`: replicates undergo the same rearrangement
* around `0`: unrelated rearrangements
* negative: replicates move in opposing directions

This is useful for identifying the non-reproducible analyses you mentioned.

---

# 24. Gene-level compensation table

```{R}
compensation_gene <- redistribution_sample %>%

  filter(
    !Gene %in%
      CONTROL_GENES
  ) %>%

  group_by(
    Gene,
    LBP_Family,
    Class
  ) %>%

  summarise(

    n =
      n_distinct(
        SampleKey
      ),

    MedianClassPct =
      median(
        ClassMolPct,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    RefClassPct =
      median(
        RefClassPct,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    MedianClassDeltaPP =
      median(
        ClassDeltaPP,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    MedianAbsClassDeltaPP =
      median(
        AbsClassDeltaPP,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    MedianRedistributionPct =
      median(
        RedistributionPct,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    IQRRedistributionPct =
      IQR(
        RedistributionPct,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%

  left_join(
    profile_agreement,
    by =
      c(
        "Gene",
        "Class"
      )
  )
```

---

# 25. Define whether the class itself is stable

```{R}
compensation_gene <- compensation_gene %>%

  mutate(

    AllowedClassDeviationPP =
      pmax(
        CLASS_STABILITY_MIN_PP,
        CLASS_STABILITY_RELATIVE *
          RefClassPct
      ),

    ClassStabilityRatio =
      MedianAbsClassDeltaPP /
      AllowedClassDeviationPP,

    ClassStable =
      ClassStabilityRatio <= 1,

    StrongRedistribution =
      MedianRedistributionPct >=
      MIN_REDISTRIBUTION_PERCENT,

    ReproducibleProfile =
      !is.na(
        ProfileAgreement
      ) &
      ProfileAgreement >=
        MIN_PROFILE_AGREEMENT,

    CompensationCandidate =
      n >=
        MIN_REPLICATES &
      ClassStable &
      StrongRedistribution &
      ReproducibleProfile
  )
```

---

# 26. Rank compensation candidates

I would not treat this score as statistics; it is simply a useful ranking function.

```{R}
compensation_gene <- compensation_gene %>%

  mutate(

    CompensationScore =

      MedianRedistributionPct *

      pmax(
        ProfileAgreement,
        0
      ) /

      (
        1 +
        ClassStabilityRatio
      )
  ) %>%

  arrange(
    desc(
      CompensationScore
    )
  )
```

Print candidates:

```{R}
compensation_gene %>%

  filter(
    CompensationCandidate
  ) %>%

  select(
    Gene,
    LBP_Family,
    Class,
    n,
    MedianClassPct,
    RefClassPct,
    MedianClassDeltaPP,
    MedianRedistributionPct,
    ProfileAgreement,
    CompensationScore
  ) %>%

  print(
    n = Inf
  )
```

---

# 27. Main compensation plot

This may be the single most useful plot in the new analysis.

```{R}
ggplot(
  compensation_gene,
  aes(
    x =
      ClassStabilityRatio,
    y =
      MedianRedistributionPct
  )
) +

  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 1,
    linetype = 2
  ) +

  geom_hline(
    yintercept =
      MIN_REDISTRIBUTION_PERCENT,
    linetype = 2
  ) +

  geom_point(
    aes(
      size =
        pmax(
          ProfileAgreement,
          0
        )
    ),
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +

  geom_text_repel(

    data =
      compensation_gene %>%
      filter(
        CompensationCandidate
      ),

    aes(
      label =
        paste(
          Gene,
          Class,
          sep = " / "
        )
    ),

    max.overlaps = Inf,
    size = 3
  ) +

  labs(

    title =
      "Potential compensatory lipid remodelling",

    subtitle =
      "Upper-left: class abundance remains stable while saturation composition changes reproducibly",

    x =
      "Change in class abundance / tolerated change\n(<1 = class relatively stable)",

    y =
      "% of saturation profile redistributed",

    size =
      "Replicate\nagreement"
  )
```

The quadrant you care most about is:

**upper left**.

That means:

> total abundance of the class barely changed, but its molecular composition changed substantially.

That is exactly the phenotype I would call a candidate **compensatory remodelling mechanism**.

---

# 28. Inspect biological replicates of the strongest candidates

This is important before believing the score.

```{R}
TOP_COMPENSATION_HITS <- compensation_gene %>%

  filter(
    CompensationCandidate
  ) %>%

  slice_max(
    CompensationScore,
    n = 30
  ) %>%

  transmute(

    Gene,
    Class,

    Hit =
      paste(
        Gene,
        Class,
        sep = " | "
      )
  )
```

```{R}
compensation_replicates <-
  redistribution_sample %>%

  inner_join(
    TOP_COMPENSATION_HITS,
    by =
      c(
        "Gene",
        "Class"
      )
  )
```

```{R}
ggplot(
  compensation_replicates,
  aes(
    x = Hit,
    y =
      RedistributionPct
  )
) +

  geom_point(
    position =
      position_jitter(
        width = 0.12
      ),
    size = 2.5
  ) +

  geom_text_repel(
    aes(
      label =
        SampleID
    ),
    size = 2.5,
    max.overlaps = Inf
  ) +

  coord_flip() +

  labs(
    title =
      "Replicate-level saturation remodelling",
    subtitle =
      "Use this plot to identify single-sample outliers before interpreting a candidate",
    x = NULL,
    y =
      "% saturation profile redistributed"
  )
```

If one LTP looks interesting solely because one replicate is enormous, add that sample to:

```{R}
EXCLUDE_SAMPLE_KEYS
```

and rerun.

---

# Part E — Which saturation bins drive the compensation?

# 29. Plot the actual DB rearrangement

For the top compensation candidates:

```{R}
candidate_profiles <- sat_difference %>%

  inner_join(
    TOP_COMPENSATION_HITS,
    by =
      c(
        "Gene",
        "Class"
      )
  )
```

Median changes:

```{R}
candidate_profiles_gene <- candidate_profiles %>%

  group_by(
    Hit,
    Gene,
    Class,
    DBbin
  ) %>%

  summarise(

    MedianDeltaPP =
      median(
        BinDeltaPP,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{R}
ggplot(
  candidate_profiles_gene,
  aes(
    x = DBbin,
    y =
      MedianDeltaPP,
    group = Hit
  )
) +

  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = 2
  ) +

  geom_line() +

  geom_point() +

  facet_wrap(
    ~ Hit,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +

  labs(
    title =
      "Direction of saturation compensation",
    x =
      "Double bonds per lipid molecule",
    y =
      "Change in class composition\n(percentage points)"
  )
```

Now you can distinguish patterns such as:

```text
DB0 ↓
DB1 ↓
DB4 ↑
DB6+ ↑
```

from:

```text
DB0 ↑
DB1 ↑
DB4 ↓
```

These are mechanistically very different compensatory responses.

---

# Part F — Resolved individual-chain saturation

This is complementary to `Total_tail_bend`.

For example:

```text
PC(18:1/18:1)
```

has `Total_tail_bend = 2`, but contains **two monounsaturated chains**, not one PUFA.

So I would also analyse each resolved chain.

---

# 30. Convert tails to long format

```{R}
tail1 <- species %>%

  transmute(

    SampleKey,
    Gene,
    Group,
    LBP_Family,
    SampleID,
    Extraction,
    Roster,
    Class,
    LipidSpecies,
    nmol,

    TailPosition = 1,

    Tail =
      as.character(
        Tail_1
      ),

    ChainLength =
      Tail1Length,

    ChainDB =
      Tail1DB
  )


tail2 <- species %>%

  transmute(

    SampleKey,
    Gene,
    Group,
    LBP_Family,
    SampleID,
    Extraction,
    Roster,
    Class,
    LipidSpecies,
    nmol,

    TailPosition = 2,

    Tail =
      as.character(
        Tail_2
      ),

    ChainLength =
      Tail2Length,

    ChainDB =
      Tail2DB
  )


chains <- bind_rows(
  tail1,
  tail2
) %>%

  filter(
    !is.na(
      ChainDB
    )
  ) %>%

  mutate(

    ChainSaturation =
      case_when(

        ChainDB == 0 ~
          "Saturated",

        ChainDB == 1 ~
          "1 DB",

        ChainDB >= 2 ~
          "2+ DB"
      ),

    ChainSaturation =
      factor(
        ChainSaturation,
        levels =
          c(
            "Saturated",
            "1 DB",
            "2+ DB"
          )
      )
  )
```

I use `"2+ DB"` rather than `"PUFA"` here because some chains may be sphingoid bases or ether-linked chains rather than conventional fatty acids.

---

# 31. Chain-equivalent amounts

One nmol:

```text
PC(16:0/20:4)
```

contributes:

```text
1 nmol saturated chain
1 nmol 4-DB chain
```

Therefore:

```{R}
chain_profile <- chains %>%

  group_by(
    SampleKey,
    Gene,
    Group,
    LBP_Family,
    SampleID,
    Class,
    ChainSaturation
  ) %>%

  summarise(

    ChainNmol =
      sum(
        nmol,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%

  group_by(
    SampleKey,
    Class
  ) %>%

  mutate(

    ChainPct =
      100 *
      ChainNmol /
      sum(
        ChainNmol,
        na.rm = TRUE
      )
  ) %>%

  ungroup()
```

---

# 32. Median chain-saturation composition

```{R}
chain_profile_gene <-
  chain_profile %>%

  group_by(
    Gene,
    LBP_Family,
    Class,
    ChainSaturation
  ) %>%

  summarise(

    MedianChainPct =
      median(
        ChainPct,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Heatmap:

```{R}
chain_profile_gene %>%

  mutate(
    Feature =
      paste(
        Class,
        ChainSaturation,
        sep = " | "
      )
  ) %>%

  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = Feature,
      y = Gene,
      fill =
        MedianChainPct
    )
  ) +

  geom_tile() +

  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name =
      "Chain\n%"
  ) +

  labs(
    title =
      "Resolved-chain saturation",
    subtitle =
      "Calculated independently within each lipid class",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +

  theme(
    axis.text.x =
      element_text(
        angle = 90,
        hjust = 1,
        size = 7
      ),

    axis.text.y =
      element_text(
        size = 6
      )
  )
```

---

# 33. Resolved-chain unsaturation index

```{R}
chain_metrics <- chains %>%

  group_by(
    SampleKey,
    Gene,
    Group,
    LBP_Family,
    SampleID,
    Class
  ) %>%

  summarise(

    ChainUnsaturationIndex =
      weighted.mean(
        ChainDB,
        w = nmol,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    MeanResolvedChainLength =
      weighted.mean(
        ChainLength,
        w = nmol,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    PolyunsaturatedChainPct =
      100 *
      sum(
        nmol[
          ChainDB >= 2
        ],
        na.rm = TRUE
      ) /
      sum(
        nmol,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    SaturatedChainPct =
      100 *
      sum(
        nmol[
          ChainDB == 0
        ],
        na.rm = TRUE
      ) /
      sum(
        nmol,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

This is the metric I would use if you specifically want to say:

> this LTP knockout shifts PC toward polyunsaturated acyl chains.

The `TotalDB` analysis alone cannot make that distinction reliably.

---

# Part G — Look explicitly for SFA ↔ MUFA ↔ PUFA compensation

This is another useful way to phrase the biology.

Suppose:

```text
total PE abundance = unchanged

SFA PE ↓
MUFA PE ↓
PUFA PE ↑
```

That is a very clean remodelling phenotype.

Median chain profile:

```{R}
chain_compensation <- chain_profile %>%

  group_by(
    Gene,
    Class,
    ChainSaturation
  ) %>%

  summarise(

    MedianChainPct =
      median(
        ChainPct,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Plot one class:

```{R}
plot_chain_saturation <- function(class_name) {

  chain_compensation %>%

    filter(
      Class ==
        class_name
    ) %>%

    ggplot(
      aes(
        x =
          ChainSaturation,
        y =
          MedianChainPct,
        group = Gene
      )
    ) +

    geom_line(
      alpha = 0.25
    ) +

    geom_point(
      alpha = 0.4
    ) +

    labs(
      title =
        paste(
          class_name,
          "resolved-chain saturation"
        ),
      x = NULL,
      y =
        "% of resolved chains"
    )
}
```

Example:

```{R}
plot_chain_saturation("PC")
plot_chain_saturation("PE")
```

## How I would interpret this analysis

The most important distinction is between **abundance** and **remodelling**.

Imagine these two phenotypes:

| KO    |   PC total | Saturation redistribution |
| ----- | ---------: | ------------------------: |
| LTP-A |       −40% |                        5% |
| LTP-B | ~unchanged |                       28% |

`LTP-A` mainly affects **how much PC exists**.

`LTP-B` is potentially much more interesting from a compensation perspective: the cell maintains PC abundance, but substantially changes **what kind of PC it makes**.

I would therefore prioritize the output from `compensation_gene`, especially LTP–class combinations with:

* `ClassStabilityRatio < 1`
* high `MedianRedistributionPct`
* `ProfileAgreement` approaching 1
* the same phenotype visible in all biological replicates
* support from the resolved-chain analysis.

The resolved-chain analysis also lets you distinguish a very important case:

**PC(18:1/18:1) → PC(16:0/20:2)**

Both molecules contain two total double bonds, so a simple `Total_tail_bend` analysis sees essentially no difference. But the chain analysis detects the change from **two MUFA chains to one saturated + one PUFA chain**. That kind of hidden rearrangement may be particularly relevant for LTP knockouts because it could preserve average membrane unsaturation while profoundly changing lipid packing, oxidation sensitivity, and downstream metabolism.

For your library, I would probably use the **class-composition heatmap + saturation-feature heatmap + compensation plot** as the three main screen-level figures, then drill into individual PC/PE/SM/TAG profiles for the strongest hits.
